full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J: The question involved in this Rule is whether the appellate Court below has the power to review its own judgment under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the appeal having arisen from a proceeding u/s. 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-emption. 

 3. Mr. Abu Taber Chowdhury, learned Advocate for the petitioner, does not challenge the merit of the order passed on review. He challenge the very jurisdiction of the lower appellate Court to review its own order. He submits that the appellate Court below exercised the power of the appellate Court because the provisions of a special statue, namely, section 96(12) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act conferred on it the powers of an appellate Court. No power to review the appellate decree or order has been granted to the appellate Court by the said special statue. Mr. Chowdhury submits that both the right of appeal and the right of review are substantive rights, and not merely procedural rights, and unless a special Act or statute confers the right of review specifically, no appellate Court, assuming jurisdiction under a special Act or statute can exercise the right of review under Order 47 rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure 

 10. I am in respectful agreement with the ratio dividend of the aforesaid decision. The appellate Court below assumed jurisdiction to hear and dispose of the miscellaneous appeal not because the jurisdiction was conferred by the Code of Civil Procedure, but because section 96(12) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act conferred jurisdiction upon the Civil Court. In deciding whether a review of the appellate order of decree will lie or not, it is immaterial how the appellate Court below came to exercise the jurisdiction, Section 114 (a) and (b) set down only one yardstick—whether the order 'or decree of which a review is sought for is appealable under the Code or not. If it is appealable and no appeal has been preferred, the case will fall under clause (a) of section 114; if it is not, the case will fall under clause (b). In the present case no second appeal is provided for in the Code itself against the appellate decree or order. It falls squarely under clause (b) section 114.
